mcqs.q: Mucositis of the maxillary sinus refers to:
opts: Thickening of the sinus mucous membrane (>3 mm) from inflammation
A fracture of the sinus wall
mcqs.explain: In mucositis the normally ~1 mm respiratory lining thickens 10–15× (>3 mm) due to infection or allergy.

mcqs.q: The normal thickness of the maxillary sinus mucous membrane is about:
mcqs.explain: The respiratory lining is normally about 1 mm thick; in mucositis it thickens to >3 mm (10–15×).

mcqs.q: Sinusitis is defined as:
opts: Inflammation of the mucosa of the sinus
mcqs.explain: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinus mucosa; pansinusitis involves all the sinuses simultaneously.

mcqs.q: Acute sinusitis is defined as inflammation lasting:
mcqs.explain: Acute = up to 4 weeks; subacute = 4–12 weeks; chronic = over 12 weeks.

mcqs.q: Which dental cause can lead to maxillary sinusitis?
opts: An infected maxillary premolar or first molar
An impacted wisdom tooth in the mandible
mcqs.explain: Infected maxillary premolars/first molars (whose roots are near the sinus floor) can cause maxillary sinusitis.

mcqs.q: A classic symptom of acute maxillary sinusitis is:
opts: A sense of cheek fullness and pain on bending forward
mcqs.explain: Acute sinusitis causes cheek fullness/pain on bending forward, nasal block, pain referred to upper teeth, tenderness on tapping the anterior antral wall and fever.

mcqs.q: On a radiograph, acute sinusitis classically shows:
opts: An air-fluid level with a horizontal border
mcqs.explain: Fluid occupies the inferior sinus and appears radiopaque; the border between the radiopaque fluid and radiolucent air is horizontal (air-fluid level).

mcqs.q: Pain from acute maxillary sinusitis is often REFERRED to the:
mcqs.explain: Pain over the upper jaw may be referred to the gums or the maxillary premolar/molar teeth.

mcqs.q: Chronic sinusitis differs from acute in that it is typically:
opts: Nonspecific and painless, with foul purulent discharge
mcqs.explain: Chronic sinusitis is nonspecific and painless, with foul purulent discharge, nasal blockage, loss of voice resonance and insomnia.

mcqs.q: Which imaging is especially useful for evaluating CHRONIC sinusitis?
mcqs.explain: CT is valuable in evaluating chronic sinusitis (with Water's view, transillumination and culture).

mcqs.q: The medical management of sinusitis includes:
opts: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, decongestants, analgesics and steam inhalation
mcqs.explain: Medical management: broad-spectrum antibiotics, decongestants (drainage), analgesics, steam inhalation and hot fomentation.

mcqs.q: Antral lavage is performed by inserting a cannula through the:
opts: Inferior meatus, then irrigating and draining the sinus
mcqs.explain: In antral lavage a cannula is inserted via the inferior meatus; warm water is irrigated and drains out through the ostium with the sinus exudate.

mcqs.q: Intranasal antrostomy creates:
opts: A drainage window/opening in the inferior meatus
mcqs.explain: Intranasal antrostomy creates a window/opening in the inferior meatus to facilitate sinus drainage.

mcqs.q: The Caldwell-Luc operation gains entry into the maxillary sinus via the:
mcqs.explain: The Caldwell-Luc operation enters the maxillary sinus via the canine fossa, combined with nasal antrostomy for drainage.

mcqs.q: A complication of maxillary sinusitis is:
opts: Orbital cellulitis or osteomyelitis of the maxilla
mcqs.explain: Complications include orbital cellulitis, osteomyelitis of the maxilla and middle-ear infections.

mcqs.q: An oroantral fistula is:
opts: An unnatural communication between the oral cavity and the maxillary sinus
mcqs.explain: An oroantral fistula is an abnormal communication between the mouth and the maxillary sinus, usually after extraction of an upper tooth.

mcqs.q: The MOST common cause of an oroantral fistula is:
opts: Extraction of an upper posterior tooth (root forced through the floor)
mcqs.explain: Extraction of an upper tooth (often with blind instrumentation forcing a root through the floor) is the commonest cause; trauma and malignancy are others.

mcqs.q: A sign of an oroantral fistula is:
opts: Regurgitation of liquids through the nose and unilateral epistaxis
mcqs.explain: Signs include regurgitation of liquids, infraorbital soft-tissue oedema, food/fluid entering the antrum and unilateral epistaxis.

mcqs.q: To test for an oroantral communication, you ask the patient to:
opts: Hold the nose and breathe out — bubbles appear in the socket
mcqs.explain: Holding the nose and breathing out forces air through any communication, producing bubbles in the extraction socket.

mcqs.q: A tooth/root displaced into the maxillary sinus appears radiographically as:
opts: A radiopaque mass (enamel/dentin/pulp) near the floor with a break in the floor
mcqs.explain: A displaced root shows as a radiopaque mass with layers of enamel/dentin/pulp near the sinus floor, with a break in the sinus floor.

mcqs.q: A retained root left in the sinus for a long time may cause:
mcqs.explain: A root remaining in the sinus for a long time can cause sinusitis; it should be located and removed (buccal flap or Caldwell-Luc).

mcqs.q: Mucositis is usually discovered because it is:
opts: Asymptomatic and found on a routine radiograph (a radiopaque band)
mcqs.explain: Mucositis is usually asymptomatic, discovered on routine radiographs as a radiopaque band paralleling the bony wall; treatment is removal of the cause.

saqs.q: Classify the diseases of the maxillary sinus.
saqs.a: Intrinsic: inflammatory (mucositis, sinusitis, polyps, antroliths) and neoplasms (osteoma; SCC). Extrinsic: periostitis, odontogenic cysts/tumours, and trauma (dental structures displaced into the sinus).
Inflammatory thickening of the sinus lining (>3 mm, normally ~1 mm). Usually asymptomatic; seen as a radiopaque band paralleling the bony wall; treated by removing the cause.

saqs.q: List the clinical features of acute maxillary sinusitis.
saqs.a: Cheek fullness/pain on bending forward, nasal block, pain referred to upper premolars/molars, tenderness on tapping the anterior wall, nasal discharge, fever; X-ray shows an air-fluid level.

saqs.q: Outline the surgical management of sinusitis.
saqs.a: Antral lavage (cannula via inferior meatus), intranasal antrostomy (drainage window), and the Caldwell-Luc operation (entry via the canine fossa); treat any dental infection.

saqs.q: Define an oroantral fistula and list its causes and signs.
saqs.a: An abnormal communication between mouth and sinus. Causes: upper tooth extraction (root through floor), trauma, malignancy. Signs: regurgitation of liquids, infraorbital oedema, unilateral epistaxis.

saqs.q: How is a tooth/root displaced into the sinus identified and managed?
saqs.a: Radiographically a radiopaque mass (enamel/dentin/pulp) near the floor with a break in the floor; if retained it causes sinusitis. Removed by buccal flap or Caldwell-Luc surgery.

saqs.q: List the complications of maxillary sinusitis.
saqs.a: Orbital cellulitis, osteomyelitis of the maxilla, and middle-ear infections.
